s1.syndrome_frame: Gradual onset of a bony hard, fixed, and lobulated chest mass in a child
salient_findings: Swelling on the right anterior chest
key_facts: Swelling first appeared as a pea-sized nodule three years earlier
Lesion gradually increased to 0.5 cm in diameter
No pain, tenderness, or respiratory symptoms
Overlying skin is normal and freely mobile
Bony outgrowth arising from the lateral aspect of the right sixth rib on radiograph

shortlist.label: Osteochondroma
shortlist.why_kept: Bony outgrowth arising from the rib, consistent with osteochondroma

shortlist.label: Chondroma
shortlist.why_kept: Possible cartilaginous origin of the bony hard mass

shortlist.label: Osteoma
shortlist.why_kept: Bony hard, fixed mass could be an osteoma

shortlist.label: Fibrous dysplasia
shortlist.why_kept: Gradual onset and bony hard mass could be consistent with fibrous dysplasia

shortlist.label: Multiple hereditary exostoses
shortlist.why_kept: Family history not mentioned, but multiple hereditary exostoses could be a consideration given the age and presentation

raw.rationale: The presence of a bony outgrowth arising from the lateral aspect of the right sixth rib on radiograph, along with the description of the mass being bony hard and fixed to the underlying rib, is consistent with osteochondroma, a type of benign bone tumor that grows on the surface of bones.

rejected.label: Chondroma
rejected.why: Chondroma typically presents as a cartilaginous tumor within the bone, not as a bony outgrowth from the surface of the bone.

rejected.label: Osteoma
rejected.why: Osteoma is a benign bone tumor, but it is typically smaller and more often found in the skull or facial bones, not arising from the ribs.

rejected.label: Fibrous dysplasia
rejected.why: Fibrous dysplasia involves the replacement of normal bone with fibrous tissue, which does not match the description of a bony outgrowth in this case.

rejected.label: Multiple hereditary exostoses
rejected.why: This condition involves multiple osteochondromas and is hereditary, but the vignette only describes a single lesion and does not mention a family history of the condition.
